claim: Mutations in KLHL40, an E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin3 (CUL3) substrate-specific adapter protein, result in severe congenital nemaline myopathy.
source: Mutations in KLHL40, an E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin3 (CUL3) substrate-specific adapter protein, result in severe congenital nemaline myopathy, but the events that initiate the pathology and the mechanism through which it becomes pervasive remain poorly understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this relationship.

claim: Global proteomics during skeletal muscle development revealed extensive remodeling of functional modules linked with sarcomere formation, energy, biosynthetic metabolic processes, and vesicle trafficking.
source: Global proteomics during skeletal muscle development revealed extensive remodeling of functional modules linked with sarcomere formation, energy, biosynthetic metabolic processes, and vesicle trafficking.
evidence: This claim is supported by the proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Combined analysis of klh40 mutant muscle proteome and ubiquitylome identified thin filament proteins, metabolic enzymes, and ER-Golgi vesicle trafficking pathway proteins regulated by ubiquitylation during muscle development.
source: Combined analysis of klh40 mutant muscle proteome and ubiquitylome identified thin filament proteins, metabolic enzymes, and ER-Golgi vesicle trafficking pathway proteins regulated by ubiquitylation during muscle development.
evidence: This is supported by the combined proteomic and ubiquitylome data analysis.

claim: KLHL40 acts as a regulator of ER-Golgi anterograde trafficking through ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation of secretion-associated Ras-related GTPase1a (Sar1a).
source: Our studies identified a role for KLHL40 as a regulator of ER-Golgi anterograde trafficking through ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation of secretion-associated Ras-related GTPase1a (Sar1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including ubiquitylation assays and protein interaction studies.

claim: In KLHL40-deficient muscle, defects in ER exit site vesicle formation and downstream transport of extracellular cargo proteins result in structural and functional abnormalities.
source: In KLHL40-deficient muscle, defects in ER exit site vesicle formation and downstream transport of extracellular cargo proteins result in structural and functional abnormalities.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and RUSH assay data.

claim: More than 50% of all causes of fetal akinesia are of neuromuscular origin, involving all points along the neuromuscular axis.
source: More than 50% of all causes of fetal akinesia are of neuromuscular origin, involving all points along the neuromuscular axis (motor neurons, peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junction, and the skeletal muscle regulatory and contractile apparatus; Ravenscroft et al., 2013; Oates et al., 2013; Vogt et al., 2008; Nowak et al., 1999; Pelin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At least 30 causative genes have been identified in fetal akinesia, arthrogryposis, and severe congenital myopathies conditions.
source: At least 30 causative genes have been identified in these conditions (Ravenscroft et al., 2018; Ravenscroft et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) regulates the relative abundance and functional modifications of proteins during multiple stages of myogenesis.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) regulates the relative abundance and functional modifications of proteins during multiple stages of myogenesis (Hnia et al., 2019; Piccirillo et al., 2014; Jirka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in genes regulating ubiquitination and protein turnover processes result in sarcomeric disarray and functional deficits in skeletal muscle.
source: The importance of UPS in skeletal muscle development has also been identified in human diseases where mutations in genes regulating ubiquitination and protein turnover processes result in sarcomeric disarray and functional deficits (Ravenscroft et al., 2013; Gupta et al., 2013; Frosk et al., 2002; Olivé et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations or deletions of sarcomeric genes affect the structure and function of surrounding organelles.
source: Mutations or deletions of sarcomeric genes affect the structure and function of surrounding organelles, and similarly, defects in other organelles in myofibers also affect sarcomere structure and function (Reimann et al., 2003; Voit et al., 2017; Fatkin et al., 2000; De Gasperi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The sarcomere and surrounding organelles act as interconnected hubs that engage in extensive communication during skeletal muscle development and maintenance.
source: This suggests that the sarcomere and surrounding organelles act as interconnected hubs that engage in extensive communication during skeletal muscle development and maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on the effects of mutations in sarcomeric genes on organelles.

claim: The KLHL40-CUL3 ubiquitin ligase complex stabilizes sarcomeric thin filament proteins such as leimodin3 (LMOD3) and nebulin (NEB) by ubiquitylation through in vitro studies.
source: KLHL40 is a substrate-specific adaptor of the E3 ubiquitin ligase CUL3, and the KLHL40-CUL3 ubiquitin ligase complex has previously been shown to stabilize the sarcomeric thin filament proteins such as leimodin3 (LMOD3) and nebulin (NEB) by ubiquitylation through in vitro studies (Garg et al., 2014), however, the in vivo relevance remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior in vitro studies.

claim: klhl40a mutant zebrafish developed a myopathic phenotype with leaner bodies during the developmental transition from juvenile (1.5 months) to adult stage (3.0 months).
source: During the developmental transition from juvenile (1.5 months) to adult stage (3.0 months), the klhl40a mutants developed a myopathic phenotype with leaner bodies, whereas klhl40b were phenotypically indistinguishable from +/+ control siblings at this age (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by visual observation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: klhl40b mutant zebrafish were phenotypically indistinguishable from control siblings at the adult stage.
source: During the developmental transition from juvenile (1.5 months) to adult stage (3.0 months), the klhl40a mutants developed a myopathic phenotype with leaner bodies, whereas klhl40b were phenotypically indistinguishable from +/+ control siblings at this age (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by visual observation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: klhl40a mutant fish showed a significant decrease in maximum swimming speed (Umax) at the adult stage (3 months) compared to control siblings.
source: The Umax values showed a significant decrease in klhl40a mutants compared to +/+ control siblings at the adult stage (3 months), indicating reduced endurance capacity of the klhl40a deficient fish.
evidence: This is supported by swimming performance data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No differences in maximum swimming speed (Umax) were observed between control and klhl40a mutants at the juvenile stage (1.5 months).
source: No differences in the Umax values were observed between control and klhl40a mutants at the juvenile stage (1.5 months).
evidence: This is supported by swimming performance data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Control fish survived to 24 months of age, whereas most klhl40a mutant fish died between 9 and 12 months.
source: Control fish survived to 24 months of age, whereas most of the klhl40a mutant fish died between 9 and 12 months.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Loss of klhl40a leads to a myopathic phenotype, as observed in patients with KLHL40 variants.
source: These data show that loss of klhl40a leads to a myopathic phenotype, as observed in patients with KLHL40 variants (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of zebrafish phenotype data with patient phenotypes from literature.

claim: Both sarcomere width and height were significantly reduced in klhl40a mutant skeletal muscle compared to controls at the adult stage.
source: Both sarcomere width (w) and height (h) were significantly reduced in the klhl40a in comparison to +/+controls at the adult stage (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: SR-ER vesicles in klhl40a mutant skeletal muscle were dilated compared to control muscle and displayed an accumulation of membrane-bound structures (10–100 nm) in close proximity.
source: SR-ER vesicles in the mutant skeletal muscle were dilated compared to the control muscle and displayed an accumulation of membrane-bound structures (10–100 nm) in close proximity (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Mitochondria in klhl40a mutant skeletal muscle were rounder and displayed an electron dense-matrix compared to controls.
source: Mitochondria in the skeletal muscle of the klhl40a mutant muscle were rounder and displayed an electron dense-matrix compared to the controls (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: klhl40a mutant muscle showed large gaps in the adjacent myofibers in the ECM region compared to controls.
source: Compared to the controls, mutant muscle showed large gaps in the adjacent myofibers in the ECM region.
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: No significant ultrastructural changes in the sarcomere or SR-ER region were observed during the juvenile stage in klhl40a skeletal muscle.
source: No significant ultrastructural changes in the sarcomere or SR-ER region were observed during the juvenile stage in the klhl40a skeletal muscle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Klhl40a is required to regulate sarcomere size, intracellular membrane homeostasis, and ECM stability in skeletal muscle.
source: These data indicate that Klhl40a is required to regulate sarcomere size, intracellular membrane homeostasis, and ECM stability in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the ultrastructural defects observed in klhl40a mutant muscle.

claim: A total of 8,268 proteins were quantified across 16 samples in the proteomic analysis.
source: A total of 8,268 proteins were quantified across these 16 samples, and PCA showed the grouping of the different replicates from each age and experimental genotype group (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data analysis.

claim: The proteome-transcriptome correlation analyses revealed a high degree of discordance (78%) between transcript-protein pairs.
source: The proteome-transcriptome correlation analyses revealed a high degree of discordance (78%) between transcript-protein pairs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of proteomic and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most differential proteomic changes in Klhl40a mutant muscle emerge during the juvenile (pre-symptomatic) state.
source: Most differential proteomic changes in the Klhl40a mutant muscle emerge during the juvenile (pre-symptomatic) state.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data analysis showing changes at 1.5 months.

claim: Proteomic changes in Klhl40a mutant muscle are primarily static during disease onset and progression.
source: These changes are primarily static during disease onset and progression.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of proteomic data at 1.5 and 3 months.

claim: Gene expression is subject to complex post-translational regulation in vivo, resulting in dynamic remodeling in normal skeletal muscle development.
source: This indicates that gene expression is subject to complex post-translational regulation in vivo, resulting in dynamic remodeling in normal skeletal muscle development.
evidence: This is inferred from the discordance between transcriptome and proteome data.

claim: The skeletal muscle developmental process exhibited enrichment with increased abundance at the pre-symptomatic state in klhl40a mutant muscle compared to controls.
source: The skeletal muscle developmental process exhibited enrichment with increased abundance at the pre-symptomatic state in the klhl40a mutant muscle compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Many proteins expressed in differentiating myotubes during early sarcomere assembly were either absent or exhibited low levels in terminally differentiated mature skeletal muscle.
source: Many of these proteins were expressed in differentiating myotubes during early sarcomere assembly. They were either absent or exhibited low levels in the terminally differentiated mature skeletal muscle (Obscn, Nexn, Ilk, Vcl, Fxr1, Synpo2l, Tnnt2, Flnc, Pdlim5, Smyd1, Unc45, Mybpc1, Lamb2, Cav1, Alpk3, Pleca, and TnnT1) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data and established knowledge of muscle development.

claim: Sarcomeric proteins associated with mature myofibers exhibited significantly less abundance in klhl40a mutant muscle at both stages.
source: Hierarchical clustering also revealed that sarcomeric proteins associated with mature myofibers exhibited significantly less abundance in mutant muscle at both stages.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Klhl40-deficient skeletal muscle exhibit a defect in the terminal differentiation of skeletal muscle with increased levels of early sarcomeric and reduced abundance of late sarcomeric proteins.
source: This suggests that Klhl40-deficient skeletal muscle exhibit a defect in the terminal differentiation of skeletal muscle with increased levels of early sarcomeric and reduced abundance of late sarcomeric proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing differential expression of early and late sarcomeric proteins.

claim: Glucose uptake and glycolytic pathway enzymes were increased in klhl40a mutant muscle during the juvenile stage compared to controls.
source: Glucose uptake (hexokinase) and glycolytic pathway enzymes (Pygma, Pygmb, Eno3, Pfkm, Aldoa, Aldob, Aldoc, Pgk1, Pgam1, Pgam2, and Pkmb) (Supplementary file 4) were increased in the mutant muscle during the juvenile stage compared to controls (pre-symptomatic stage).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: Categories associated with cellular metabolism showed amino acid and lipid metabolism enrichment, mitochondrial respiration, and nucleotide metabolism in klhl40a mutant muscle at both stages.
source: Categories associated with cellular metabolism also showed amino acid and lipid metabolism enrichment, mitochondrial respiration, and nucleotide metabolism in mutant muscle at both stages (Figure 4A red and yellow nodes, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pathways regulating bioenergetics balance in skeletal muscle are altered in klhl40a mutant muscle.
source: This suggests that pathways regulating bioenergetics balance in skeletal muscle are altered in the mutant muscle (Supplementary files 1 and 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing changes in metabolic enzymes.

claim: Sarcomere remodeling in stress or disease states is associated with altered metabolic states by increasing glycolytic and mitochondrial proteins.
source: Sarcomere remodeling in stress or disease states is associated with altered metabolic states by increasing glycolytic and mitochondrial proteins (Toepfer et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Changes in the ubiquitylome of klhl40a mutant muscle were established before functional and structural changes were observed in skeletal muscle.
source: Similar to the dynamics of changes observed in the proteome, changes in the ubiquitylome of mutant muscle were established before functional and structural changes were observed in skeletal muscle (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the ubiquitylome data analysis.

claim: Nebulin is a direct ubiquitination target of Klhl40-Cul3 complex.
source: Previous studies have shown nebulin is a direct ubiquitination target of Klhl40-Cul3 complex and was identified in cluster 1, validating our hypothesis (Garg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and identification in the ubiquitylome data.

claim: Most proteins exhibited changes in Ub-sites that correlated positively at the pre-symptomatic and symptomatic stages.
source: Most proteins exhibited changes in Ub-sites that correlated positively at the pre-symptomatic and symptomatic stages. (Figure 3C and E and Supplementary files 1–6).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of ubiquitylome data shown in Figure 3C and E.

claim: Ubiquitylation marks by the Klhl40-Cul3 complex and potentially other ubiquitylation enzymes are robust and unidirectional in the disease state.
source: This suggests that ubiquitylation marks by the Klhl40-Cul3 complex and potentially other ubiquitylation enzymes are robust and unidirectional in the disease state.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of proteins showing significant enrichment of Ub-sites in different directions.

claim: Many ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitylases showed differential expression between control and klhl40a mutant muscle.
source: As many ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitylases showed differential expression between control and mutant muscle, these proteins could be direct targets of many of these enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: Highly ubiquitylated proteins in klhl40a mutant muscle had decreased abundance.
source: Integration with the proteome data revealed that these highly ubiquitylated proteins had decreased abundance in mutant muscle (Tmod4, Tnni2, Tpm2, Cfl2, Myom2).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of proteomic and ubiquitylome data.

claim: Many highly ubiquitylated proteins are localized to thin filaments and contribute to nemaline myopathy.
source: Many of these highly ubiquitylated proteins are localized to thin filaments and contribute to nemaline myopathy, indicating other components of the ubiquitin proteasomal pathways may cause increased ubiquitylation and abnormal degradation of sarcomere proteins in mutant muscle and affect thin filaments stability (Figure 4C–D, Supplementary files 8-9).
evidence: This is inferred from the ubiquitylome data and knowledge of nemaline myopathy.

claim: Sar1a, glycolytic proteins (Pkmb, Aldo, Aldob), and sarcomeric proteins (Ttn, Tnnt2, Nckipsd) are potential targets of the Klhl40-Cul3 complex.
source: Finally, to identify potential targets of the Klhl40-Cul3 complex, analysis of fold changes of reduced Ub-sites and abundance of their cognate proteins in response to Klhl40a deficiency in opposite directions identified Sar1a (vesicle trafficking protein), glycolytic proteins (Pkmb, Aldo, Aldob) and sarcomeric proteins (Ttn, Tnnt2, Nckipsd).
evidence: This is supported by integrated analysis of proteomic and ubiquitylome data.

claim: Reduced ubiquitylation of Sar1a, glycolytic proteins, and sarcomeric proteins suggests these may be directly regulated through ubiquitylation by the Klhl40-Cul3 complex.
source: While the proteomic analysis indicated altered sarcomeric and glycolytic proteins might contribute to disease pathology in Klhl40a deficiency, reduced ubiquitylation of these proteins, suggest these may be directly regulated through ubiquitylation by the Klhl40-Cul3 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined proteomic and ubiquitylome data.

claim: SAR1A is a small GTPase required to assemble COPII vesicles at endoplasmic reticulum exit sites (ERES) by recruiting the SEC23/24 complex for protein trafficking.
source: SAR1A is a small GTPase required to assemble COPII vesicles at endoplasmic reticulum exit sites (ERES) by recruiting the SEC23/24 complex for the protein trafficking (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Sar1a protein levels were significantly increased in klhl40a mutant muscle.
source: While Sar1a protein levels were significantly increased, inner coat proteins of COPII vesicles Sec23b and Sec23d and Golga2 were reduced in the mutant muscle suggesting that they are co-regulated in Klhl40a deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: Inner coat proteins of COPII vesicles Sec23b and Sec23d and Golga2 were reduced in klhl40a mutant muscle.
source: While Sar1a protein levels were significantly increased, inner coat proteins of COPII vesicles Sec23b and Sec23d and Golga2 were reduced in the mutant muscle suggesting that they are co-regulated in Klhl40a deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: No changes were observed in the outer coat proteins of COPII vesicles (Sec13 and 31) in klhl40a deficiency.
source: No changes were observed in the outer coat proteins of COPII vesicles (Sec13 and 31; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Proteomics analysis showed no significant changes in the ER resident protein Sec12 or other COPII proteins, Tango1, cTAGE5, and Sec13/31 levels in Klhl40a deficiency.
source: Proteomics analysis also showed no significant changes in the ER resident protein Sec12 or other COPII proteins, Tango1, cTAGE5, and Sec13/31 levels in Klhl40a deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: Changes to vesicular trafficking proteins were regulated post-transcriptionally, as no differences were seen in these proteins at the mRNA level.
source: These changes to the vesicular trafficking proteins were regulated post-transcriptionally, as no differences were seen in these proteins at the mRNA level (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of proteomic and RNA-seq data.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed increased Sar1a protein levels in klhl40a mutant skeletal muscle compared to control.
source: Western blot analysis in control and mutant klhl40a mutant skeletal muscle protein extracts at the adult stage (3 months) confirmed increased Sar1a protein levels in the mutant skeletal muscle compared to the WT control (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Western blot validated reduced Sec24d and Golga2 in Klhl40a deficient skeletal muscle.
source: Moreover, Western blot also validated reduced Sec24d and Golga2 in Klhl40a deficient skeletal muscle. (Supplementary file 1, Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: SAR1A mRNA overexpression (50–100 ng) resulted in abnormal membrane-bound structures in the SR-ER region similar to klhl40a mutant fish.
source: Ultrastructural examination of zebrafish larvae by electron microscopy showed that SAR1A mRNA overexpression (50–100 ng) resulted in abnormal membrane-bound structures in the SR-ER region similar to klhl40a mutant fish (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Increased SAR1A protein levels in skeletal muscle result in the abnormal accumulation of ER-derived membrane-bound structures.
source: This suggests that increased SAR1A protein levels in skeletal muscle result in the abnormal accumulation of ER-derived membrane-bound structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the SAR1A overexpression experiments.

claim: Klhl40a deficient myofibers exhibited increased accumulation of Sar1a in the ER compared to controls.
source: Klhl40a deficient myofibers exhibited increased accumulation of Sar1a in the ER compared to controls (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: An increased number of Sar1a and PDI-positive foci were observed in klhl40a mutant muscle.
source: Moreover, an increased number of Sar1a and PDI-positive foci were observed in mutant muscle.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Abnormal membranous structures in klhl40a mutant muscle originated from the ER.
source: This suggests that abnormal membranous structures in the ER-SR region in the mutant muscle originated from the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the ultrastructure and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Immunofluorescence with Tango1 antibody revealed reduced ER exit sites (ERES) in Klhl40-deficient myofibers.
source: Immunofluorescence with Tango1 antibody revealed reduced ER exit sites (ERES) in Klhl40-deficient myofibers.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: klhl40a mutant myofibers showed an increased number of Tango1-positive enlarged ERES sites (~200–500 nm) (5.2 ± 1.91 %) compared to control myofibers (0.70 ± 0.39%).
source: Although the size of ERES sites showed variability in both control and mutant myofibers (50–500 nm), mutant myofibers showed an increased number of Tango1-positive enlarged ERES sites (~200–500 nm) (5.2 ± 1.91 %) compared to control myofibers (0.70 ± 0.39%).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Examination of COPII vesicle protein Sec23B showed fewer COPII vesicles in Klhl40a deficiency.
source: Examination of COPII vesicle protein Sec23B showed fewer COPII vesicles in Klhl40a deficiency
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Examination of the Golgi apparatus in Klha40a showed normal immunoreactivity in most of the myofibers (63 ± 14%) with varying amounts of GOLGA2-positive aggregates in other myofibers.
source: Finally, examination of the Golgi apparatus in Klha40a showed normal immunoreactivity in most of the myofibers (63 ± 14%) with varying amounts of GOLGA2-positive aggregates in other myofibers.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No altered autophagy markers were observed in Klhl40a deficiency.
source: As dysregulation of autophagy is associated with vesicle trafficking, we examined different autophagy markers (Atd5, Atg16l1, Atg4b, Atg9a, beclin, Lc3b, Lamp1, and Lamp2) in the proteomic data or by western blot (LC3) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). We did not observe any altered autophagy markers in Klhl40a deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No differences were observed in Bip, Calnexin, Ero1, Ireα1, CHOP, and PERK between control and klhl40a skeletal muscle by proteome or RNA-seq analysis.
source: No differences were observed in Bip, Calnexin, Ero1, Ireα1, CHOP, and PERK between control and klhl40a skeletal muscle (1.5 and 3 months) by proteome or RNA-seq analysis (3 months).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic and RNA-seq data.

claim: xbp1 mRNA spliced during UPR in the ER showed no change in klhl40a mutant muscle.
source: xbp1 mRNA spliced during UPR in the ER also showed no change in the klhl40a mutant muscle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western blot analysis of PERK showed no differences in the total PERK levels or phospho-PERK levels in Klhl40a deficiency compared to control muscle indicating a lack of UPR activation in Klhl40a deficiency.
source: Western blot analysis of PERK showed no differences in the total PERK levels or phospho-PERK levels in Klhl40a deficiency compared to the control muscle indicating a lack of UPR activation in Klhl40a deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Abnormally increased amounts of Sar1a do not result in the formation of productive COPII vesicles and contribute to abnormal vesicle formation associated with changes in crucial protein regulators of ER-Golgi vesicle trafficking.
source: These studies provide evidence that abnormally increased amounts of Sar1a do not result in the formation of productive COPII vesicles and contribute to abnormal vesicle formation associated with changes in crucial protein regulators of ER-Golgi vesicle trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence and ultrastructural data.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation assays in C2C12 cells showed SAR1A is a direct interactor of KLHL40.
source: To test if SAR1A is a direct substrate of KLHL40, we performed co-immunoprecipitation assays in C2C12 cells that showed SAR1A is a direct interactor of KLHL40 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A gradual decrease in KLHL40 protein levels resulted in a concomitant increase in SAR1A protein levels in muscle cells.
source: A gradual decrease in KLHL40 protein levels resulted in a concomitant increase in SAR1A protein levels in muscle cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by overexpression assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the presence of MG132, increased stability of SAR1A was observed, suggesting that KLHL40 targets SAR1A for degradation through proteasomes.
source: To understand if the interaction between KLHL40 and SAR1A results in reduced levels of SAR1A through ubiquitylation-mediated protein degradation, we evaluated the effect of KLHL40 protein on SAR1A stability in the presence of the proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 7C). In the presence of MG132, increased stability of SAR1A was observed, suggesting that KLHL40 targets SAR1A for degradation through proteasomes.
evidence: This is supported by proteasome inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The SAR1A ubiquitylation site identified by ubiquitylome analysis is highly conserved in vertebrates.
source: Analysis of vertebrate SAR1A protein sequences revealed that the SAR1A ubiquitylation site identified by ubiquitylome analysis is highly conserved in vertebrates suggesting that SAR1A ubiquitylation in skeletal muscle may be conserved in all vertebrates (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Western blot analysis showed increased SAR1A ubiquitylation as a function of time in the presence of wild-type KLHL40 but not GST-only control.
source: Western blot analysis showed increased SAR1A ubiquitylation as a function of time in the presence of wild-type KLHL40 but not GST-only control (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variants in the N-terminal BTB domain of KLHL40 (L86P) and BACK domain (W201L) showed similar SAR1A ubiquitylation as the wild-type protein.
source: Variants in the N-terminal BTB domain of KLHL40 (L86P) and BACK domain (W201L) showed similar SAR1A ubiquitylation as the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Variants in the Kelch domains (R311L and E528K) resulted in a significant reduction in SAR1A ubiquitylation.
source: Still, variants in the Kelch domains (R311L and E528K) resulted in a significant reduction in SAR1A ubiquitylation (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Patients with loss of function or missense variants in the Kelch domains in KLHL40 may exhibit reduced SAR1A ubiquitylation.
source: As Kelch proteins bind their targets through the C-terminal Kelch domains, this suggests that patients with loss of function or missense variants in the Kelch domains in KLHL40 may exhibit reduced SAR1A ubiquitylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro ubiquitylation assay data and knowledge of Kelch protein function.

claim: KLHL40 is required for SAR1A ubiquitination in the context of muscle cells by CUL3, as no ubiquitylation was observed in the absence of KLHL40.
source: Finally, SAR1A ubiquitylation was evaluated in C2C12 cells in the presence or absence of KLHL40 with CUL3 by overexpression and immunoprecipitation assays. This showed that KLHL40 is required for SAR1A ubiquitination in the context of muscle cells by CUL3, as no ubiquitylation was observed in the absence of KLHL40 (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitylation assay data in C2C12 cells shown in Figure 7H.

claim: KLHL40-CUL3 is a regulator of SAR1A in skeletal muscle under normal conditions.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that KLHL40-CUL3 is a regulator of SAR1A in skeletal muscle under normal conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of interaction, ubiquitylation, and degradation assays.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis showed extensive immunoreactivity of procollagens intracellularly in klhl40a mutant muscle compared to control muscle.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis with intracellular muscle protein α-actinin showed extensive immunoreactivity of procollagens intracellularly in the klhl40a mutant muscle compared to the control muscle (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Collagen staining was reduced in klhl40a mutant muscle and no collagen immunoreactivity was detected intracellularly.
source: Collagen staining was also reduced in the klhl40a mutant muscle and no collagen immunoreactivity was detected intracellularly (Figure 8A arrow).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Significantly reduced levels of integrin β–1 were seen in ECM in klhl40a mutant muscle compared to control muscle.
source: While no immunostaining of another ECM protein, integrin β–1, was observed intracellularly, significantly reduced levels were seen in ECM in the klhl40a mutant muscle compared to the control muscle.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A reduced rate of ER-export of procollagen was observed in human KLHL40 knockout MB135 myoblasts compared to controls.
source: We observed a reduced rate of ER-export of procollagen in human KLHL40 knockout MB135 myoblasts compared to controls and small cargo sialyl transferase (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is supported by RUSH assay data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: KLHL40 is critical for the trafficking of large cargo proteins in skeletal muscle.
source: This suggests that KLHL40 is critical for the trafficking of large cargo proteins in the skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the RUSH assay data showing reduced procollagen trafficking.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of KLHL40 NM patient muscle showed increased immunoreactivity for SAR1A protein in most of the myofibers.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of the skeletal muscle of the KLHL40 NM muscle showed increased immunoreactivity for SAR1A protein in most of the myofibers. Many myofibers exhibited a very high level of SAR1A immunoreactivity (Figure 9A, white arrows) compared to control muscle.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: KLHL40 deficient skeletal muscle showed increased collagen within the muscle fibers, similar to klhl40a fish.
source: KLHL40 deficient skeletal muscle also showed increased collagen within the muscle fibers, similar to klhl40a fish (Figure 9A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Increased expression of SAR1A is specific to KLHL40-deficient skeletal muscle as analysis of skeletal muscle from centronuclear myopathy patients (RYR1 or MTM1 disease-causing mutations) showed no changes in the SAR1A protein levels compared to control.
source: This increased expression of SAR1A is specific to KLHL40-deficient skeletal muscle as analysis of skeletal muscle from centronuclear myopathy patients (RYR1 or MTM1 disease-causing mutations) showed no changes in the SAR1A protein levels compared to the control (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle from KLHL40 patient revealed extensive vesicle accumulation and aberrant ECM structures with reduced collagen fibers similar to Klhl40 deficient zebrafish.
source: Analysis of the ultrastructure of skeletal muscle from KLHL40 patient (c.[932G>T];[1516A>C] p.[Ag311Leu];[Thr506Pro]) revealed that in addition to nemaline bodies, extensive vesicle accumulation (arrows) and aberrant ECM structures with reduced collagen fibers (arrowhead) similar to Klhl40 deficient zebrafish were observed (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Defects in vesicle trafficking contribute to disease onset and pathology in KLHL40 deficiency in patient skeletal muscles.
source: This suggests that defects in vesicle trafficking contribute to disease onset and pathology in KLHL40 deficiency in patient skeletal muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the patient muscle analysis showing SAR1A upregulation and vesicle accumulation.

claim: Deleting Klhl40 in mice results in extensive structural damage in myofibers and neonatal lethality 2 to 3 weeks after birth.
source: Deleting Klhl40 in mice also results in an extensive structural damage in myofibers and neonatal lethality 2 to 3 weeks after birth (Garg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The human orthologue of the KLHL40 gene is duplicated in zebrafish as klhl40a and klhl40b and mapped on chromosome 2 and chromosome 24, respectively.
source: The human orthologue of the KLHL40 gene is duplicated in zebrafish as klhl40a and klhl40b and mapped on chromosome 2 and chromosome 24, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: klhl40abwg200 allele has insertion of one base (c.250_251insA; p.Val84Aspfs*36).
source: klhl40a alleles created include klhl40abwg200 with insertion of one base (c.250_251insA; p.Val84Aspfs*36) and klhl40abwg201 with a two base pair deletion in exon 1 (c.251_252insTC;p.Val84Asnfs*36).
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: klhl40abwg201 allele has a two base pair deletion in exon 1 (c.251_252insTC;p.Val84Asnfs*36).
source: klhl40a alleles created include klhl40abwg200 with insertion of one base (c.250_251insA; p.Val84Aspfs*36) and klhl40abwg201 with a two base pair deletion in exon 1 (c.251_252insTC;p.Val84Asnfs*36).
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: klhl40abwg200 and klhl40abwg201 alleles result in frameshift mutations and are predicted to result in truncations in the N terminal BTB domain of the Klhl40a protein.
source: These alleles result in frameshift mutations and are predicted to result in truncations in the N terminal BTB domain of the Klhl40a protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: klhl40bbwg202 allele had insertion of one base (c.674_675insC; p.Arg225Profs*14) in exon 1.
source: For klhl40b, a CRISPR-edited allele (klhl40bbwg202) had insertion of one base (c.674_675insC; p.Arg225Profs*14) in exon 1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: klhl40bbwg202 allele is predicted to result in a frameshift mutation and truncation of the Klhl40b protein in the BACK domain.
source: klhl40bbwg202 allele is predicted to result in an frameshift mutation and truncation of the Klhl40b protein in the BACK domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Both klhl40a and klhl40b alleles exhibited similar klhl40a and klhl40b mRNA levels, respectively, in comparison to +/+ siblings.
source: Both klhl40a and klhl40b alleles exhibited similar klhl40a and klhl40b mRNA levels, respectively, in comparison to +/+ siblings.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a 50% decrease in Klhl40 protein levels in both klhl40a and klhl40b alleles compared to control and complete absence of Klhl40 protein in klhl40a/klhl40b double knockout fish.
source: Western blot analysis with a KLHL40 antibody that recognizes both Klhl40a and Klhl40b proteins revealed a 50% decrease in Klhl40 protein levels in both alleles compared to control and complete absence of Klhl40 protein in klhl40a/klhl40b double knockout fish (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: klhl40a and klhl40b alleles result in the loss of Klhl40 protein in the mutant zebrafish.
source: This suggests that klhl40a and klhl40b alleles result in the loss of Klhl40 protein in the mutant zebrafish.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data.

claim: klhl40a and klhl40b mutant embryonic (2dpf) and larval fish (5dpf) did not exhibit gross morphological defects.
source: klhl40a and klhl40b mutant embryonic (2dpf) and larval fish (5dpf) did not exhibit gross morphological defects in any of the mutants examined.
evidence: This is supported by visual observation.

claim: The discrepancy between klhl40 morphants and mutants could be due to genetic compensatory mechanisms by other Kelch protein-coding genes or other modifier genes.
source: The discrepancy between the morphants and mutants could be due to genetic compensatory mechanisms by other Kelch protein-coding genes or other modifier genes as described by several studies (El-Brolosy et al., 2019; Sztal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotype in mutants compared to morphants and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: klhl40a and klhl40b exhibit overlapping expression in skeletal muscle.
source: klhl40a and klhl40b exhibit overlapping expression in skeletal muscle, and a lack of phenotype in klhl40b mutants suggested functional redundancy similar to a large number of duplicated genes (Ravenscroft et al., 2013; Taylor and Raes, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A lack of phenotype in klhl40b mutants suggested functional redundancy similar to a large number of duplicated genes.
source: klhl40a and klhl40b exhibit overlapping expression in skeletal muscle, and a lack of phenotype in klhl40b mutants suggested functional redundancy similar to a large number of duplicated genes (Ravenscroft et al., 2013; Taylor and Raes, 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotype in klhl40b mutants and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CUL3-dependent ubiquitylation dynamically regulates the trafficking of large COPII carriers.
source: CUL3-dependent ubiquitylation is previously shown to dynamically regulate the trafficking of large COPII carriers (Jin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: KLHL12, another substrate-specific adapter for CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase forms a complex with CUL3 which ubiquitylates SEC31 leading to an increase in COPII vesicle size to accommodate large procollagen molecules for secretion in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC).
source: KLHL12, another substrate-specific adapter for CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase forms a complex with CUL3 which ubiquitylates SEC31 leading to an increase in COPII vesicle size to accommodate large procollagen molecules for secretion in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC; Jin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A subset of procollagens is directed towards lysosomal degradation to remove excess procollagen from cells through the autophagy pathway.
source: While most procollagens are trafficked through the secretory pathway, a subset is directed towards lysosomal degradation to remove excess procollagen from cells through the autophagy pathway (Omari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Recent studies in skin fibroblasts have shown that the CUL3-KLHL12 complex is involved in routing procollagens to lysosomes to regulate intracellular collagen levels.
source: Recent studies in skin fibroblasts have shown that the CUL3-KLHL12 complex is involved in routing procollagens to lysosomes to regulate intracellular collagen levels (Moretti et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of CUL3 neddylation which is critical for the ubiquitylation activity still led to the formation of large COPII vesicles by the CUL3-KLHL12 complex, which is required for the secretion of procollagens.
source: Moreover, inhibition of CUL3 neddylation which is critical for the ubiquitylation activity still led to the formation of large COPII vesicles by the CUL3-KLHL12 complex, which is required for the secretion of procollagens.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: KLHL12 is expressed at very low levels in normal skeletal muscle compared to other cells and tissue types.
source: KLHL12 is expressed at very low levels in normal skeletal muscle compared to other cells and tissue types (http://gtexportal.org).
evidence: This is supported by reference to GTEx portal data.

claim: No differential changes in Klhl12 and the target protein Sec31 were identified in Klhl40a deficiency.
source: We did not identify any differential changes in Klhl12 and the target protein Sec31 in Klhl40a deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: No changes in the protein levels of autophagy markers were observed in Klhl40a deficiency at the disease states examined.
source: Moreover, no changes in the protein levels of autophagy markers were observed in Klhl40a deficiency at the disease states examined.
evidence: This is supported by the proteomic data.

claim: ERES functions as an inter-organelle transport apparatus that actively modulates its shape and size while directing diverse cargo types to Golgi and increases in size during active transport.
source: ERES functions as an inter-organelle transport apparatus that actively modulates its shape and size while directing diverse cargo types to Golgi and increases in size during active transport (Weigel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The increase in the size of ERES sites in Klhl40a deficiency could be a compensatory mechanism to enhance the secretory flux.
source: As Klhl40a deficiency resulted in reduced procollagen trafficking from ER, this increase in the size of ERES sites could be a compensatory mechanism to enhance the secretory flux.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed increase in ERES size and reduced procollagen trafficking.

claim: Reduced or limited amounts of Sec16b and COPII proteins in klhl40a mutant myofibers may underlie a reduced number of ERES sites and COPII vesicles.
source: Despite the presence of increased Sar1A levels in Klhl40a-deficient myofibers, reduced or limited amounts of other proteins, such as Sec16b and COPII proteins in the mutant myofibers may underlie a reduced number of ERES sites and COPII vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic and immunofluorescence data.

claim: SAR1A is 90% identical to SAR1B, and these proteins exhibit overlapping and unique functions with different biochemical properties in COPII assembly.
source: SAR1A is 90% identical to SAR1B, and these proteins exhibit overlapping and unique functions with different biochemical properties in COPII assembly (Melville et al., 2020; Georges et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SAR1B specifically regulates chylomicron trafficking in the small intestine.
source: While SAR1B specifically regulates chylomicron trafficking in the small intestine, both proteins are required for the trafficking of cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 protein and efficient ER export of procollagens and may be able to compensate for each other function for the trafficking of common proteins (Jones et al., 2003; Levic et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012; Cutrona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both SAR1A and SAR1B are required for the trafficking of cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 protein and efficient ER export of procollagens and may be able to compensate for each other function for the trafficking of common proteins.
source: While SAR1B specifically regulates chylomicron trafficking in the small intestine, both proteins are required for the trafficking of cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 protein and efficient ER export of procollagens and may be able to compensate for each other function for the trafficking of common proteins (Jones et al., 2003; Levic et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2012; Cutrona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Downregulation of Sar1a levels in skeletal muscle may be able to restore the procollagen trafficking defects in Klhl40a deficiency.
source: In Klhl40a deficiency, increased amounts of Sar1a resulted in the formation of abnormal ER-derived membrane-bound structures and decreased procollagens trafficking; therefore, downregulation of Sar1a levels in skeletal muscle may be able to restore the procollagen trafficking defects.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed effects of increased Sar1a.

claim: Defects in ECM are directly associated with contracture in many neuromuscular diseases.
source: Defects in ECM are directly associated with contracture in many neuromuscular diseases.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Vesicle trafficking dysregulation is associated with neurodegenerative and skeletal disorders.
source: Vesicle trafficking dysregulation is associated with neurodegenerative and skeletal disorders, and our findings open new avenues on this pathway in neuromuscular diseases.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Klhl40a directly regulates vesicle trafficking and contributes to disease pathology.
source: Our studies identified structural defects in skeletal muscle in Klhl40a deficiency and showed that Klhl40a directly regulates vesicle trafficking and contributes to disease pathology.
evidence: This is supported by the combined experimental data from the study.

claim: Dynamic fine-tuning of the cellular proteome by ubiquitylation is critical for muscle function.
source: Overall, we provide a comprehensive temporal proteomic landscape during skeletal muscle growth and disease development, and dynamic fine-tuning of the cellular proteome by ubiquitylation is critical for muscle function.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive proteomic and ubiquitylome data.

claim: Approaches aiming to inactivate pro-disease pathways and activate protective pathways may be a promising therapeutic strategy for at least this form of NM.
source: Given the several pathways in which KLHL40 is involved, approaches aiming to inactivate pro-disease pathways and activate protective pathways may be a promising therapeutic strategy for at least this form of NM.
evidence: This is speculated based on the identification of multiple pathways affected in KLHL40 deficiency.
